en: The *Buddha Speaks the Sūtra of the Mango Girl Jīva*,
translated by An Shigao of the Later Han.
When the Buddha was in the world, a mango tree grew spontaneously within the royal park of King Vijayī.
The branches and leaves were lush and abundant, and the fruit was even larger; it possessed a radiant luster and an extraordinary fragrance and flavor.
The king truly cherished these *nālikera* fruits, and none but the noble and beautiful women of the palace were permitted to eat them.

In that country there was a brahmin householder whose wealth was beyond counting and who was peerless in the entire land; moreover, he was intelligent and profoundly learned, his talent and wisdom surpassing all others, such that the king held him in high esteem and appointed him as a great minister.
The king invited the brahmin; when the meal was finished, he presented him with a single mango as a reward.
Seeing that the mango was exceptionally fragrant and exquisite, the brahmin asked the king, "Under this mango tree, might there be a small sapling that I might beg for?"
The king said, "There are many small seedlings; I feared they would obstruct the large trees, so I have removed them.
If you wish to have them, I shall give them to you now."
He immediately gave him a single pear tree.

Having received it, the brahmin returned home and planted it; he irrigated it morning and evening, and day by day it grew larger, its branches and twigs becoming lush and beautiful. After three years, it bore fruit; the luster and size of the fruit were like those of the royal family’s pears.
The brahmin was greatly delighted and thought to himself:

"My family's wealth is countless and not inferior to that of the king; it was only because I lacked this *nai* that I considered myself his inferior. Now that I have obtained it, I am no longer inferior to the king."
He immediately took some to eat, but it was extremely bitter and astringent, such that it was utterly inedible.
The brahmin became even more distressed and, withdrawing to reflect, thought:
"This must simply be because the soil here lacks fertility and moisture."
He then took the milk of a hundred cows and gave it to drink to a single cow; he then took the milk of that cow, boiled it down to produce ghee, and poured it over the root of the mango tree.
He irrigated it day after day until the following year, when its fruit became sweet and delicious, like the *nālikera* (jackfruit) of a royal household;
yet, by the side of the tree, a gall suddenly grew, as large as a clenched fist, increasing in size day by day.
The brahmin thought to himself:
"Suddenly this tumor has appeared; I fear it will obstruct its fruit.
I wish to cut it away, yet I fear I might harm the tree."

He contemplated this day and night, lingering in indecision; then, from within a joint, a branch suddenly sprouted, pointing straight upward—tall, straight, and well-proportioned, rising above the treetop to a height of seventy feet from the ground. Its tip then branched out in various directions, spreading around like an inverted canopy, its flowers and leaves so lush and beautiful that they surpassed those of the parent tree.
The brahmin marveled at this, wondering,
"I do not know what there might be upon these branches.
He then constructed a wooden platform, climbed up, and looked.
Looking up into the midst of the canopy formed by the branches, he saw a pool of water that was both clear and fragrant; it was as if there were many flowers, their colors vivid and bright.
Peering beneath the flowers, he saw a young girl within the waters of the pool.
The brahmin took her in his arms and returned home to raise her, naming her Āmrapālī.
When she reached the age of fifteen, her appearance was so upright and beautiful that she was peerless in all the world, and her fame spread to distant lands.
There were seven kings who came simultaneously to the brahmin’s abode, seeking to marry the daughter of the *nāga* tree as their queen.
The brahmin was greatly terrified, not knowing to whom he should give her; he therefore erected a high tower within his garden, placed the daughter atop it, and went out to address the kings, saying:
"This girl was not born of me; she emerged spontaneously from the top of the *nāga* tree. I do not know whether she is a goddess, a nāga, or a spirit-woman."
Is it a demonic entity?
Now that seven kings have come together to seek it, if I were to give it to one king, the other six would surely be enraged; I dare not begrudge it to them.

"The girl is now on the upper floor of the pavilion in the garden; let the various kings deliberate among themselves, and whoever deems her suitable may take her for himself—this is not within my control."
Thereupon, the seven kings disputed among themselves, their clamor unresolved until the evening.
That night, King Bimbisāra entered through a secret tunnel, ascended the tower, and stayed there with him for the night.
As she was about to depart at dawn, the woman said to him:
"Your Majesty has condescended to approach me with your august presence; now you abandon me and go away again. If I should have a son, he would be of royal lineage—to whom should he be entrusted?"
The king said, "If it is a son, you shall return him to me;
if it is a daughter, I shall give her to you."
The king immediately removed the seal of his golden ring from his hand and gave it to the daughter of Nai as a token of faith.
He then went out and said to his ministers:

"I have already obtained the daughter of Nai and stayed with her for one night; however, there was nothing extraordinary about her, as she was just like an ordinary woman, and for that reason, I did not take her."
Within King Piṇḍola’s army, everyone shouted "Ten Thousand Years!
and said, "Our King has already obtained the daughter of Nanda.
When the six kings heard this, they each returned to their own places.
Later, the woman gave birth to a son; at the time of his birth, he emerged holding a pouch of needles and medicinal drugs in his hands.
The brahmin said, "This is the son of a king, yet he holds medical instruments; he must surely be a king of physicians."
His name was Jīvaka.

By the time he reached the age of eight, he was exceptionally intelligent and highly talented; his learning and mastery of the written texts surpassed all his peers. When he played with the children of his neighborhood, his mind was constantly disdainful toward them, considering them inferior to himself.
The children all reviled him together,
saying, "Son of a fatherless man, born of a harlot, how dare you insult us?
Jīvaka was struck with astonishment and remained silent, offering no reply.
He returned home and asked his mother, saying, "I looked at those sons of yours; none of them are as good as I am, yet you instead revile me, saying:
'You son of a fatherless man!'"
"Where is my father now? His mother replied,
"Your father is none other than King Prasenajit."
Jīva said, "King Bimbisāra is in the kingdom of Rājagṛha, five hundred li from here; by what cause could he have fathered me?
If it is as my mother says, what proof can there be?"
The mother immediately took out a seal-ring and showed it to him, saying, "This is your father’s ring.
Jīvaka examined it and saw that it bore the seal-mark of King Bimbisāra; he then took the ring and went to the kingdom of Rājagṛha.
He entered the palace gate directly, and no one there stopped him; arriving before the king, he paid his respects and knelt for a long time, saying to the king:

"I am a prince, born of Princess Nāī. This year I am eight years old, and only now have I come to know that I am of the Great King’s lineage. Therefore, carrying this signet ring as my seal of proof, I have traveled far to return home."
When the king saw the inscription on the seal, he recalled his former vow; realizing that this was indeed his son, he felt a poignant sense of pity and made him the crown prince.
After two years had passed, King Ajātaśatru was born, and Jīvaka addressed the king, saying:
"At the time of my birth, I held a pouch of needles and medicine in my hand; therefore, I am destined to be a physician."
"Although the King regards me as his crown prince, this is not what I desire;
for the King has now fathered a legitimate son who should inherit the noble succession, and I wish instead to go forth and study the art of medicine."
The king immediately granted his permission.
The king said, "If you do not become a crown prince, you shall not consume the royal stipend in vain; you must study the way of medicine."
The king immediately issued a decree to the foremost physicians in the kingdom, commanding them to exhaust their skills in instructing him.
However, Jīvaka spent his time only in play and never underwent formal study. The teachers rebuked him, saying:
"Medical arts are base and vulgar; they truly are not fit for the Supreme Son of the King to learn. Nevertheless, the life of the Great King must not be disregarded or abandoned."
"Since receiving Your Majesty's decree, many days and months have passed, yet the Crown Prince has not accepted even half a word of instruction. If the King were to question me, how should I answer?"

Jīvaka said, “I was born with the marks of a physician in my hands; therefore, I informed the Great King that I would renounce my noble status and seek to study the medical arts. How could I possibly be indolent as to require a teacher’s supervision?”
"It is simply because the teachings of these various masters are not worth studying.
He then took up the *Bencao* (Pharmacopoeia), the *Yaofang* (Prescriptions for Medicines), and various sutras on the channels and pulses (*mai*), and posed detailed questions to his teacher.

The masters were at their wit's end and had no answer; they all descended from their seats and paid homage to Jīvaka, kneeling with palms joined and saying, "Today we have learned in secret that the Prince is divine and sagely; he truly is beyond our reach."

"The matters we have just asked about are all points of doubt that have remained unresolved throughout our teachers' successive lifetimes. We pray that the Prince will explain them in full detail, so as to untie the knots within us that have bound us since birth."
Jīva then explained its meaning for them; the physicians were filled with joy, all rose once more, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet in salutation, and received his teaching.
Thereupon, Jīvaka set out to treat illnesses, and every case he treated was healed; his fame spread throughout the kingdom.

Later, wishing to enter the palace, he encountered a young boy carrying firewood before the palace gate. As Jīvaka gazed at him, he saw all the boy’s five viscera, intestines, and stomach with complete clarity.
Jīva thought to himself:
"The Herbal Classic states that there is a 'King of Medicines' tree; when light shines from its exterior into the interior, one can see the internal organs of a person.
Among this child's firewood, might there not be such a King of Medicines?"
He immediately went to ask the boy,
"How much do you want for the firewood?
The boy replied:
"Ten coins. He then hired the boy for ten coins; when the boy set down the firewood, it became even more pitch-black, and he could no longer see into its belly.
Jīvaka thought further to himself:

"Without knowing which among these bundles is the King of Medicine," he untied both bundles and took each piece one by one to place upon the child's abdomen; seeing nothing at all, he would set it aside and take another.

In this way, he exhausted both bundles of firewood until there remained only a small branch barely a foot long. He tried taking this to shine upon the belly, and immediately the interior was clearly visible. Jīvaka was greatly delighted, knowing for certain that this small branch was the King of Medicine, and he returned all the child's firewood to him.
The boy, having already received the money, returned the firewood as it was before and departed with joy.
At that time, in the kingdom, there was the daughter of a householder (gṛhapati) who was fifteen years old; on the very day she was about to be married, she suddenly died from a headache.
Upon hearing this, Jīvaka went to her house and asked the girl’s father,
"What illness has this daughter constantly suffered that it has even led to death?
The father replied:
"The woman suffered from a slight headache that has increased in severity over the months and days; this morning it flared up more intensely than usual, leading to her death.

Jīvaka then approached and examined her head with the King of Medicines; he saw parasitic worms, large and small, reproducing one another in numbers reaching several hundred, boring into and devouring her brain. Because the brain was completely consumed, she died.
He then used a golden knife to slit open the head and extracted all the worms, placing them in a jar.
He applied three kinds of divine ointments to the wounds: one was to mend the injuries between the bones eaten by the worms;
another was to regenerate the brain.
There was one who treated external sword wounds.
He said to the girl’s father, “Ensure she remains calm and do not allow her to be startled; she shall recover and return to her former state within seven days. On that day, I shall come back again.”
As soon as Jīvaka had departed, the woman’s mother wept and cried out:
"My son has died a second death! How could there be a physician who would slit open the head and extract the brain, only for him to be restored to life?"
"Father, how can you bear to command another to take your son away like this?

The father stopped him and said, "Jīvaka was born holding a needle and medicine; he has renounced his royal status to practice as a physician solely for the sake of all living beings' lives. He is the King of Physicians ordained by Heaven—how could he possibly act falsely!"
I entrusted you with these words, saying:
"Be careful not to cause him alarm.
Yet now you have done the opposite, weeping and crying out to startle him; will you thereby cause this child to lose his life?
Upon hearing her father’s words, the mother ceased weeping and attended to him with care, remaining in a state of tranquility for seven days.
At dawn on the seventh day, the girl blew upon him and he awoke, saying as if rising from sleep:
“I no longer have a headache at all; my body is entirely at ease.”
"Who protected me so that I might become like this?
His father said, "You were already dead before; it was Jīvaka, the King of Physicians, who came to protect you, broke open your head to extract the worm, and thereby enabled you to regain life."
He then opened the jar and took out the worms to show them to her.
Upon seeing this, the woman was struck with great terror and, feeling deeply fortunate, said:
"Jīvaka’s divine power is truly such as this; how shall I repay his kindness?"
The father said,
"Jīvaka made an appointment with me, saying:
'I shall come today.'"
Thereupon, in a brief moment, Jīvaka arrived. The woman was filled with great joy; she went out to welcome him, prostrated herself at his feet, and knelt for a long time with palms joined, saying:
"I wish to serve as Jīvaka’s maidservant for the rest of my life, providing offerings to repay the kindness of being restored to life."
Jīvaka said, “I am a physician who travels everywhere to treat illnesses; I have no fixed dwelling. What use would I have for a slave girl?
If you truly wish to repay my kindness, give me five hundred ounces of gold.”
"I do not need this gold either. The reason I seek it is that when ordinary people study the Way, it is the rule that they should offer thanks to their teacher.
Although my teacher has had nothing to teach me, I was once his disciple; now that I have obtained your gold, I shall give it to him."
The woman then offered five hundred ounces of gold to Jīvaka; Jīvaka accepted it and gave it to his teacher, then addressed the king:
"I shall go home for a brief visit to see my mother and will arrive at the kingdom of Vaiśālī."
In the kingdom, there was also the son of a householder (gṛhapati) who was fond of martial arts; he fashioned a wooden horse over seven feet high and practiced riding it every day as a beginner.
Just as he had mounted his horse, after practicing for a long time, he suddenly lost his balance and fell to the ground, dying instantly.

When Jīvaka heard of this, he went there and used the "Medicine King" to examine the interior of his abdomen; he saw that the man's liver was inverted and twisted toward the back, and because his vital energy was constricted and blocked, he had died.

Furthermore, he used a golden knife to cut open his abdomen and reached in with his hand to arrange the organs; once he had returned the liver to its forward position, he applied three kinds of divine ointments:
one to heal the places where his hands had grasped and torn, one to regulate the flow of the vital breaths, and one to close the wound caused by the knife.
Having finished his instructions, he said to the father, "Be careful not to startle him; he shall recover in three days.

The father followed these instructions, tending to the child in silence and stillness. When the third day arrived, the boy exhaled deeply and awoke; appearing as if rising from sleep, he immediately sat up.
In a short while, Jīvaka also arrived; the boy joyfully went out to meet him, prostrated himself with his head at his feet, knelt for a long time, and said:
"I wish to become Jīvaka’s slave and serve you for the rest of my life, in order to repay the kindness of being restored to life."
Jīvaka said, "I am a physician who travels everywhere to treat the sick; the houses of my patients vie to employ me as their servant, so what need have I for a slave?"
"My mother raised me with great toil and hardship, yet I have not yet repaid her for her kindness through offerings.
If you wish to express gratitude for my kindness, you may give me five hundred taels of gold to repay my mother's debt of gratitude."
Thereupon, taking the gold, he presented it to the daughter of Nai and returned to the kingdom of Rājagṛha.
Jīvaka restored these two men to life, and his fame spread throughout the world; there was no one who did not hear of or know it.
Furthermore, to the south there is a great kingdom, eight thousand *li* from Rājagṛha; Piṣapa and all the small kingdoms are its subjects.

Its king has been ill for many years without recovery, and he constantly suffers from fits of rage; he kills people at the mere glance of an eye. He kills anyone who looks up at him, and kills anyone who lowers their head and does not look up. He kills anyone who walks slowly, and kills anyone who runs swiftly.
The attendants on his left and right did not know where to place their hands or feet.
Whenever the physician prepared medicine, he would immediately suspect it was poisonous and kill the patient.
The number of palace women, courtiers, and members of the medical staff killed by him, both before and after, is beyond counting.
His illness grew increasingly severe; a poisonous heat assailed his heart, causing distress, fullness, and shortness of breath, as if his body were being consumed by fire.
Upon hearing that there was one named Jīvaka, he immediately issued a written decree, commanding King Bimbisāra to summon Jīvaka.

When Jīvaka heard that the king intended to execute many physicians, he was greatly terrified; yet because King Bimbisāra took pity on his youth and feared he might be killed, he wished not to send him, while Jīvaka himself feared being put to death.
Father and son remained together, grieving day and night, not knowing what plan to adopt.
At that time, King Bimbisāra took Jīvaka with him and went together to question the Buddha.
The Buddha told Jīvaka:
"In a previous life, you and I made a vow together that we would both protect all people from illness in the world.
I was to treat internal diseases, while you were to treat external diseases. Now that I have attained Buddhahood, you have appeared before me in accordance with our original vow."
"This king’s illness is grave; he has come from afar to welcome you—how can you not go?
Go quickly to rescue and protect him, and employ skillful means so that his illness will surely be cured and the king will not kill you."

Jīvaka, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, went to the king’s location. He examined the king’s pulse and used the King of Medicines to illuminate his condition; he saw that within the king’s five viscera and hundred vessels, the blood and qi were turbulent, entirely consisting of the venom of snakes and scorpions pervading his entire body.
Jīvaka said to the king:

"The King’s illness can be treated; with treatment, recovery is assured. However, it is necessary that you be granted an audience with the Queen Mother so that we may consult together on the preparation of the medicine. If you do not see the Queen Mother, the medicine will ultimately not be completed."

When the King heard these words, he did not understand their cause and was deeply provoked to anger; however, being afflicted by his own illness and having long heard of Jīvaka’s reputation, he went out to welcome him from afar, hoping for certain benefit. Furthermore, thinking that as a mere child he could have no other treacherous intent, he suppressed his rage and listened, immediately dispatching a eunuch in green robes to lead him in to see the Empress Dowager.
Jīvaka said to the Empress Dowager:
"The King's illness can be cured; we must now compound a medicine. You should keep the formula secret and not let it become known; you ought to request that those around you be cleared away."
The Empress Dowager immediately dispatched a maidservant and a eunuch to depart.
Jīvaka then asked the Empress Dowager:

"Just now, when I examined the King's illness, I observed that the blood and qi within his body were entirely the venom of snakes and scorpions; he does not seem to be human. Who, then, is this King’s biological son?"
"The Empress Dowager told me the truth, and I am now able to treat you;
had she not told me, I would not have treated you, and your illness would not have been cured.
The Empress Dowager said:

"In the past, while I was sleeping during the day in the Hall of Golden Pillars, a being suddenly came and pressed down upon my body. At that time, I was in a state of bewilderment, as if dreaming yet awake, appearing like one in a nightmare; thus, I became intimate with it."
Suddenly he awoke and saw a large wasp, over three chi in length, flying away from him; he then realized he was pregnant, and the king was indeed the offspring of this wasp.
"I have been ashamed of this and never spoke of it, yet you, young man, have now perceived it; how marvelous and divine!
If this illness can be cured, I pray that by the King's command you be entrusted with its treatment.
As for treating it now, what medicine should be used?"
Jīva said, "There is only the *sarpis-manda* (the finest essence of clarified butter).
The Empress Dowager said:

"Stop! Young man, be careful not to speak of this *amṛta* (clarified butter). The King greatly detests the scent of *amṛta* and also detests the very name of *amṛta*. Previously, hundreds of thousands of people have died from speaking the word 'amṛta' while sitting before him. If you speak of it now, he will surely kill you.
Give this to the King to drink; it will never go down. I pray you, use some other medicine instead."
Jīva said, "Clarified butter (ghṛta) cures poison; it is precisely because the disease of poisoning is loathsome that one hears of clarified butter.
If Your Majesty’s illness were slight, or if it were caused by some other poison, there would be other medicines capable of curing it."
"The venom of the scorpion is already grave and has already circulated throughout Your Majesty’s body; were it not for *amṛta* (clarified butter), it could never be neutralized.

We shall now boil and refine it to transform it into water, rendered odorless and tasteless. Your Majesty will not perceive it, and you shall drink it of your own accord. Once the medicine has entered, you will surely be cured; there is no need for concern."
He then went out and saw the King, saying:
"I entered just now and saw the Empress Dowager; I have already informed her of the medicinal formula. It shall now be prepared, and it will be completed in fifteen days."
"Now I have five wishes; if Your Majesty grants them, my illness may be cured, but if you do not grant them, my illness will not be cured.
The king asked:
"What are the five wishes? Jīvaka replied:
"The first is that I wish to obtain new garments from the king’s inner storehouse, never yet worn upon a body, to clothe myself."
Second, I vow that I alone may enter and exit the palace gates without anyone stopping me;
third, I vow that I may enter daily to see the Empress Dowager and the Queen, without being forbidden or rebuked;
fourth, I vow that when the King drinks the medicine, he shall drink it all at once and not stop midway.
Fifth, he wished: "May I obtain a white elephant eight thousand *li* in height to ride upon.
When the king heard this, he said in great anger:
"You rat-child!"
"How dare you ask for these five boons?
Explain them quickly; if you cannot explain them, I shall kill you right now.
Why do you seek new clothes from me?"
"Did he wish to kill me, and so put on my clothes to falsely assume my form?

Jīvaka replied, "To prepare medicine, one ought to be pure and observe the precepts of purification. However, it has been a long time since I last came, and my garments were all covered in dust and grime; thus, I truly wished to obtain the King's clothes to wear while preparing the medicine."
The King then understood his meaning and said: "This is most excellent!
Why do you further wish to enter and exit the palace gates yourself without being subject to prohibitions or reprimands?"
"Do you intend to lead troops here to attack and kill me? Jīvaka replied,

"Your Majesty has previously employed various physicians, yet you have always harbored suspicions toward them, never entrusting them with full confidence, and furthermore, you have executed them and refused to take their medicines."

The ministers, both high and low, all said, "The King will surely kill us again; however, the King’s illness is now extremely severe, and we fear that outsiders may harbor rebellious intentions and cause a disturbance.

If you allow me to enter and exit at my own discretion without being restricted or censured, then everyone, both high and low, will know that the King trusts me and will certainly take my medicine. His illness will surely be cured, and they will not dare to harbor thoughts of rebellion."
The king said, "Excellent!
For what reason do you wish to enter alone every day to see my mother and see my wife?"
"Do you wish to commit lewd immorality?

Jīvaka replied, "The King has killed many people before and after; from the high officials down to the lowly, everyone harbors fear and none wish for the King's well-being. There is no one who can be trusted."
Now, while we are compounding the medicine, he may cast poison into it during the mere blink of my eye; that I would not perceive this is no small matter.

Reflecting upon those in the world who can be trusted, there are none whose affection is equal to that of one's mother or wife; therefore, I firmly desire to enter and see the Empress Dowager and the Empress so that we may compound and decoct the medicine together. It will take fifteen days to complete, and I truly wish to enter every day to attend to the progress of the medicinal decoction.
The king said, "Excellent!
Why did you cause me to drink the medicine all at once until it was finished, not allowing me to stop midway?"
"Is it because you wish to poison me from within, fearing that I might perceive it?
Jīvaka replied, "Medicines have their prescribed proportions; their potency and flavor must correspond to one another. If these were interrupted, then the efficacy would not be sustained."
The king said, "Excellent!
For what reason do you wish to have my white elephant for you to ride?"

"This elephant is the national treasure of our country; it travels eight thousand li in a single day. It is precisely because we rely on this elephant that we have intimidated and subdued all other nations.
Do you wish to ride it because you intend to steal it back to your home and join with your father to attack our kingdom?"

Jīva said, "In the mountains of the southern border there is a divine and wondrous medicinal herb, four thousand li from here. Your Majesty, once you have taken the medicine, you should immediately obtain this herb and take it again."
"I wish to mount this white elephant and go to gather it, departing in the morning and returning by evening, so that the medicinal flavors may remain intact.
The King’s mind was greatly relieved, and he granted him permission in every respect.

Thereupon, Jīvaka refined the *sarpirmaṇḍa* (clarified butter) for fifteen days until it was transformed into something like clear water; he obtained five *śu* in total. He then presented the medicine to the Empress Dowager and the Queen, and together they carried the vessel out, saying to the King:
"Please take this. We pray that you prepare the white elephant and station it before the palace."
The king immediately granted his consent.

When the king saw the medicine, it appeared only like clear water; it had no scent or flavor at all, and he did not know it was *sarpis* (clarified butter). Furthermore, the Empress Dowager and the Queen personally supervised its preparation, believing it to be non-toxic. Thus, according to their original agreement, he consumed it all in a single dose.
Jīvaka then mounted an elephant and returned directly to his native country.

After traveling three thousand li, Jīvaka, being young in years and his strength still slight, could not endure the rapid pace; his head spun and he was utterly exhausted, so he stopped among the mountains to lie down and rest.
When the sun had passed its zenith, the king let out a belch and smelled the stench of clarified butter (sarpis). He became greatly enraged and said:
"That little mouse has mixed clarified butter into my food! I suspected why that mouse was seeking my white elephant; it was precisely because he intended to rebel and flee!"
The king had a heroic minister named Eḷu, who alone possessed such supernormal power that he could travel on foot as fast as this elephant.
He immediately called out to Eḷu:
"Go quickly after the rat and capture it alive; bring it back, and I shall personally beat it to death before my very eyes."
"By nature you have always been unable to be frugal and are greedy for food and drink; therefore, you are called a 'crow' (vāyasa).
These practitioners of medicine often delight in administering poisons; if a rat sets out food for you, be careful not to eat it!"
Having received the command, the crow went forth and caught up with him in the mountains.
The crow said, "For what reason do you take the King of All Medicines from the *sarpis* (clarified butter) and yet claim it is ordinary medicine?"
"The King has therefore sent me to summon you back. You must follow me home at once; by offering your apologies and confessing, there may still be hope for your life.
If you attempt to flee, you shall certainly be killed now and will never escape."
Jīva thought to himself:
"Although I have employed skillful means to seek this white elephant, I still cannot escape. I must now employ further skillful means; how can I simply go along with him?"
He then said to the crow, "I have not eaten since this morning;
if I return, I will surely die. Would it not be better for you to grant me a brief moment so that I may eat fruit and drink water in the mountains, and then face death with a full belly?"
Seeing that Jīvaka was a mere child, terrified of death and speaking with great distress, the crow felt pity for him and said:
"Eat quickly and we must depart; we cannot stay long."
Jīva then took a pear, bit off half of it, and placed poison under his fingernails; he then divided the remaining half and set it on the ground.
He further took a cup of water, first drank half of it, and likewise applied the poison from beneath his nails to the remainder of the water, which he then also set on the ground.
He then sighed and said:

"This water and these pears are both celestial medicines; they are both fragrant and delicious. Those who consume them will find their bodies at peace, all their ailments will be cured, and their vigor will double."

Regretting that it was not located within the capital so that the common people might all have access to it, but instead lay deep in the mountains where no one knew of it, he entered the mountains to search for that fruit.

The crow’s nature being greedy, it could not endure hunger and thirst; furthermore, having heard Jīvaka praise it as a divine medicine and seeing that Jīvaka himself had already eaten and drunk of it, the crow concluded there must be no poison. It then took the remaining pears and ate them, and drank all the remaining water. Immediately, it suffered from diarrhea as copious as a pouring stream; it fell to the ground and lay there, and whenever it attempted to rise, it would faint and fall over, unable to move again.
Jīvaka went to him and said, "If Your Majesty takes my medicine, your illness will surely be cured.
However, the power of the medicine has not yet taken effect and the remaining poison is not yet exhausted; if I go now, you will certainly kill me."
"You know nothing; you have risen with the desire to find me so as to relieve the burden upon your body, which has surely caused you this illness.
This illness is not inherently painful; be careful not to move, and it shall be cured in three days.
If you persist in rising to pursue me, you will certainly die—of this there is no doubt."
He then mounted the elephant and departed.
Jīvaka passed through a village settlement and said to the village headman:

"This is an envoy from the Great King; he has suddenly fallen ill. You must go quickly to carry him home and tend to him well. Provide him with fine bedding and give him venison porridge; take care not to let him die. If you cause him to die, the King will destroy your country."
Having finished speaking, he departed and returned to his own country.
The company commander, receiving the imperial decree, went out to welcome him and provide for his care; after three days, the poison subsided and his bowels were cleared.
The crow then returned to see the king, prostrated himself, and said:

“I am truly foolish to have defied the King’s command and, believing the words of Jīvaka, consumed his leftover fruit and water. I was struck by poison and suffered from diarrhea for three days; it is only this morning that I have recovered, yet I know I am destined to die.”

Within three days of the crow's return, the king’s illness had already healed. The king, reflecting on his own actions, regretted having sent the crow away; seeing the crow return, he was both sorrowful and joyful, saying:
"It is fortunate that you did not bring my son back immediately; had I been in a fit of rage, I certainly would have beaten him to death."
"I have received his kindness and my life has been sustained by him; yet I have instead killed him. Such a rebellious and perverse crime is no small matter.
He then repented for all those he had previously wrongfully executed, providing them with elaborate funerals, restoring their families, and bestowing wealth and property upon them.
Desiring to see Jīvaka and wishing to repay his kindness, the king immediately dispatched a messenger to welcome him.
Although Jīvaka knew that the king’s illness had already been cured, he still harbored lingering fear and was unwilling to go again.
Jīvaka again went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
A messenger has been sent from that land to summon you; may you go there?”
The Buddha told Jīvaka:
"In your past lives, you already made a great vow that you should accomplish meritorious virtues; how can you stop midway?
You must go there once more."
"You have already treated his external ailments; I, too, shall treat his internal ailments. Jīvaka then followed the messenger away.
Upon seeing Jīvaka, the king was filled with great joy; he invited him to sit beside him, took hold of his arm, and said:
"I owe my life to the grace of your benevolence; having now been restored to life, how may I repay you?"
"I shall divide my kingdom and give half to you; the palace ladies and the treasures in the storehouses shall all be divided in half. I pray that you, O Benevolent One, will accept them."
Jīvaka said, "I was originally born as a prince;

although it was a small kingdom, it was fully endowed with people, treasures, and precious things. Because I took no pleasure in governing a kingdom, I sought to become a physician. Since I must practice healing, what use would I have for land, women, or precious objects?"
"None of these are of use.
Previously, Your Majesty granted me five wishes and my external illness was cured; if you would once again grant me one more wish, my internal illness may likewise be healed."
The king said, "I shall indeed follow your benevolent instruction; I request to hear further concerning one of my wishes. Jīvaka replied:
"I pray that Your Majesty will invite the Buddha and receive from him the teachings of clarity.
He then described for the king the Buddha’s majestic and preeminent merits.
Upon hearing this, the king was filled with great joy and said:
"I now wish to dispatch the white elephant Ucchiṣṭa to welcome the Buddha; can he be brought here? Jīvaka replied, "There is no need for the white elephant.

The Buddha understands all things and knows the thoughts in people's minds from afar. You need only observe the fast and maintain purity, prepare offerings and burn incense, and from afar invite him toward you, prostrate yourself, and kneel long to make your request; the Buddha will surely come of his own accord."

The king acted according to these words. On the following day, the Buddha arrived together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus. After the meal was finished, he preached the sūtra for the king; the king’s mind was opened and liberated, and he immediately gave rise to the unsurpassed, right, and true mind of enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*). All those in the kingdom, both great and small, received the five precepts; each paid their respects and departed after performing obeisance.

Furthermore, since Princess Nanda was born with such extraordinary qualities and grew up to be exceptionally intelligent, she studied under her father and gained extensive knowledge of the scriptures, the Way, astrology, and various arts; she surpassed her father in these matters and, moreover, excelled in vocal music, her voice being like that of Brahmā.
Five hundred people in total, including various *gṛhapatis* and daughters from the families of *brahmans*, all went to follow her and study under her, regarding her as their great teacher.

The daughter of the *nyagrodha* tree constantly followed five hundred disciples to lecture on and receive the teachings of the scriptures; at times they would play together in gardens and ponds, or perform music.
The people of the country did not understand the reason for this and began to spread slanderous rumors, calling her a "prostitute" and labeling her five hundred disciples as a "prostitute's faction.
Furthermore, when Nanda was born, there were also two other girls in the country named Sumana and Pundarika, who were born at the same time.

As for the girl Sumana, she was born within a *sumana* flower. In a certain householder’s family in the country, they were constantly pressing *sumana* flowers to make fragrant oil. Beside the stone used for pressing the oil, a tumor-like knot suddenly formed, as large as a pellet; it grew day by day until it was the size of a fist, whereupon the stone burst open. Within the knot of the stone, something bright like a firefly was seen, its light shooting out and falling to the ground.

After three days it produced a *sumana* flower, and after another three days the flower fully blossomed. Within the blooming flower was a young girl; the householder took her in and raised her, naming her Sumana.
He grew up handsome and excellent, endowed with talent, brilliance, and wisdom, second only to the daughter of Nya.

At that time, there was also a brahmin’s household where blue lotuses grew spontaneously within their bathing pool; these flowers were exceptionally large and grew day by day, reaching the size of five-dou measures of grain jars.
As the flower opened, she saw a girl within it; the brahmin took her and raised her, naming her Pāṭalā.
When she grew up, she was beautiful and possessed of talent, brilliance, and wisdom, just like the daughter of Sumana.
When the various kings heard that these two daughters possessed a beauty unparalleled in the world, they all came to seek their hands in marriage.

The two daughters said, "We were not born from a womb, but emerged from within a flowering plant; thus we are unlike ordinary mortals. How could it be appropriate for us to follow the ways of worldly people and marry again?"

Hearing that the daughter of Nai was intelligent beyond compare in the world and was born as his own kinswoman, he took leave of his parents and went to serve her, seeking to become her disciple. He became wise and profoundly learned, surpassing all five hundred men.

At that time, as the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Vaiśālī, the daughter of the Mango Grove (Amrapālī) led five hundred disciples out of the city to welcome the Buddha. She prostrated herself with her head at his feet, knelt for a long time, and said:
"I pray that the Buddha will come to my garden tomorrow for a meal."
The Buddha accepted her invitation by remaining silent. The daughter of the Naga returned home to prepare the offerings.

When the Buddha entered the city, the King again came out from his palace to welcome him; having completed his prostrations, he knelt for a long time and requested that the Buddha come to the palace the following day.
The Buddha said, "The daughter of Nanda requested it first; Your Majesty followed later.
The King said:
"I am a king who has invited the Buddha with a sincere heart; I truly hope for his compassionate acceptance!
Yet this daughter of Nai is merely a courtesan who daily leads five hundred female disciples in unrighteous conduct. Why does the Buddha abandon me to respond to her invitation?"
The Buddha said:
"This woman is not a courtesan; she possesses great merit from her past lives and has already made offerings to three hundred million Buddhas.

In the past, this Nāḍikā woman was also a sister to Sumanas and Padmā; Nāḍikā was the eldest, Sumanas was next, and Padmā was the youngest. They were born into a family of great lineage, possessing abundant wealth and treasures."

The sisters led one another to collectively make offerings to five hundred bhikṣuṇīs; day after day they provided them with food and drink, as well as clothing, supplying whatever they lacked until the end of their lives.
The three made a solemn vow, saying:
"May we, in future lives, encounter a Buddha and attain spontaneous transformation-birth, not by way of a womb, remaining far removed from all defilement and impurity."
"Now, in accordance with her original vow, she has been born to meet me at this time.
Furthermore, although she formerly made offerings to bhikṣuṇīs, being the daughter of a wealthy family, her speech was arrogant and dissolute; from time to time she would mock the bhikṣuṇīs, saying:
'You practitioners have resided in this town for a long time; you must surely wish to marry.'"
"Because we were constrained by those who provided us with offerings and supervision, we were unable to indulge our own inclinations.
Therefore, we now suffer these remaining karmic retributions; though we read the sutras and practice the Way every day, we are falsely subjected to slander."

These five hundred disciples also exerted their strength together at that time to assist in making offerings; with one heart and joyful minds, they have now gathered here once more, following one another as before.

"At that time, Jīva was born as the son of a poor family. Seeing the daughter of Nai making offerings, his heart was filled with deep admiration and joy; yet, lacking the means, he would constantly sweep for the bhikṣuṇīs. Once the area had been cleaned, he would immediately form this thought:
'If only I could sweep away the filth and diseases of the bodies of all people in the world—how wonderful that would be!'"
The daughter of Nanda took pity on her poverty and, moreover, increased her efforts, constantly calling her "daughter.
When that bhikṣuṇī fell ill, she always had Jīvaka summon physicians and prepare decoctions, saying:
"May you, in future lives, together with me, obtain this merit."
Jīva welcomed these physicians, and all those he treated were healed; he then made this vow:
"May I, in future lives, become a Great King of Physicians, constantly treating the diseases of the four great elements within the bodies of all beings, so that wherever I go, all may be cured."
"Due to the causes and conditions of past lives, I have now become the son of the daughter of Nai; all this is in accordance with my original vow.
When the King heard the Buddha’s words, he knelt for a long time in repentance and postponed [the marriage] until a later day.
On the following day, the Buddha went with the bhikṣus to the mango grove of the three daughters and fully explained for them the merit of their original vows.
Upon hearing the sutra, the three daughters attained liberation; together with their five hundred disciples, they were simultaneously filled with joy and all realized the path of Arhatship.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"You should receive and uphold this, and explain it for the fourfold assembly, so that it shall not be interrupted.
All sentient beings must be careful with their body, speech, and mind; do not give rise to arrogance or negligence."
Because this woman, in a former life, mocked and teased a bhikṣuṇī, she has now been subjected to false accusations of sexual misconduct.

You should cultivate the actions of body, speech, and mind, and constantly make virtuous vows. Those who hear this should rejoice, believe, delight in, and uphold it; do not give rise to slander, lest you fall into hell, where the remaining retribution will be as an animal for hundreds of thousands of kalpas. Thereafter, when the retribution of being born as a human occurs, one will be poor and lowly, not hear the True Dharma, be born into a family of wrong views, constantly encounter evil kings, and have an incomplete physical form.
"You should practice, receive, uphold, read, and recite this, ensuring that it never ceases throughout the limits of the future.
Thus spoke the Buddha in the *Nai-nü Qipo Jing* (The Sūtra of the Maiden Jīvā).
